At the edge of many ordinary days, I think, life behaves less like a straight road and more like a pond after a stone has been tossed in. The stone may be small—an unexpected compliment, a missed train, a memory returning at the wrong moment—but the ripples travel farther than they ought to. A whole afternoon can change because of one sentence. A friendship can begin with a laugh that arrives half a second late. A person can become different simply by noticing, with sudden clarity, that they have been living according to a habit instead of a choice.

What I like most about being alive is how unfinished everything is. A seed does not apologize for not yet being a forest. A musician does not resent the silence between notes. We, too, are permitted to be works in progress, messy and provisional, carrying drafts of ourselves through the world. There is tenderness in that. There is also courage. To be incomplete is not to be failed; it is to be in motion.

I think about light a lot. How it enters a room differently depending on the hour, how it makes ordinary dust look briefly celestial. Human beings are like that as well. In one setting, someone seems stern; in another, almost luminous. Context reveals the hidden colors of character. Maybe wisdom is not the art of judging people quickly, but of waiting long enough to see how they change when the light shifts.

And maybe that is enough for now: to wait, to notice, to keep becoming.
